content: Chromates and dichromates are salts derived from chromic acid and dichromic acid, respectively. Chromate salts contain the chromate ion (CrO₄²⁻) and are characterized by their intense yellow coloration. Dichromate salts, on the other hand, contain the dichromate ion (Cr₂O₇²⁻) and exhibit a vivid orange color. In both chromate and dichromate ions, the chromium atoms are in the +6 oxidation state, which is also referred to as hexavalent chromium. These ions are strong oxidizing agents. In aqueous solutions, chromate and dichromate ions exist in a state of chemical equilibrium, interconverting depending on the pH of the solution. Chromates and dichromates are utilized in environmental analysis, particularly for measuring chemical oxygen demand (COD). However, all hexavalent chromium compounds, including chromates and dichromates, are toxic and classified as carcinogenic. When used as oxidizing agents or titrants in redox chemical reactions, these compounds are reduced to trivalent chromium (Cr³⁺), which has a distinct blue-green color. The sodium (Na⁺), potassium (K⁺), and ammonium (NH₄⁺) salts of chromates and dichromates are water-soluble granular solids and are the most commonly employed forms of these compounds in chemical applications. In contrast, chromate and dichromate salts of heavy metals, lanthanides, or alkaline earth metals are only sparingly soluble in water, limiting their practical utility. Chromate conversion coatings are applied to metals to provide corrosion protection and to enhance the adhesion of paints.
